title: Adjacency matrix: addEdge and neighbour list printing
statement:
Anbu prepares the road map of a district with n towns numbered from 0 to n-1. Every road joins two towns and can be used in both directions. The program stores the roads in an adjacency matrix, where the value 1 at the position (i, j) means that the towns i and j are joined by a road. The function addEdge records a road between two towns, and the function printList prints, for every town, the list of the towns that are joined to it by a road, in the increasing order of their numbers.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v (a road).
Output Format: n lines: town number + ":" + " neighbour" for each neighbour in increasing order (only the number and ":" when a town has no road).
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2); no self-loops or duplicate roads.
easy: Mark both matrix cells for every undirected road, then scan each row left to right to print the neighbours in increasing order.
logic: addEdge(u, v) sets adj[u][v] = 1 AND adj[v][u] = 1 (undirected!).
printList: for each i print i << ":", then for j = 0..n-1 print " " << j whenever adj[i][j] == 1.
Scanning j in increasing order automatically gives sorted neighbour lists.
algorithm: int adj[20][20] global (all zeros).
addEdge(u, v): both cells set to 1.
main: read n, m; call addEdge m times; call printList(n).
printList(int n): nested loop as above, endl after each town.
mistakes: Setting only adj[u][v] - undirected edges need BOTH cells (the classic bug in the given code).
Printing neighbours from v = 1 instead of j = 0.
Missing space before each neighbour - the format is exactly "0: 1 2 3".
note: The QB shows the two samples only as an embedded image; they were recovered and verified (see audit report).

title: Cycle detection in an undirected graph (DFS with parent)
statement:
Chandru is a plumber who checks the water pipeline of a colony. The colony has n junctions numbered from 0 to n-1, and every pipe joins two junctions. A pipeline that has a closed loop of pipes can cause a water-flow problem. A closed loop is a path that starts at a junction, uses different pipes, and comes back to the same junction. The network may have several separate parts. The program stores the pipes in an adjacency matrix, and the function hasCycle returns the message "Cycle Exists" if the network has a closed loop in any of its parts, or "No Cycle" otherwise.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v (a pipe).
Output Format: "Graph Check: " + Cycle Exists / No Cycle.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2); no self-loops or repeated pipes.
easy: DFS from every unvisited junction, carrying the parent junction; meeting an already-visited neighbour that is NOT your parent means a cycle.
logic: dfs(n, u, parent): mark u visited; for every neighbour v: unvisited -> recurse with parent = u; visited and v != parent -> cycle found.
The parent check stops the false alarm caused by the edge you just came along.
hasCycle loops over all start vertices so separate parts are all checked.
algorithm: bool dfs(int n, int u, int parent): standard recursive check as above; returns true on cycle.
string hasCycle(int n): for i = 0..n-1: if not visited and dfs(n, i, -1) return "Cycle Exists"; return "No Cycle".
main: read the graph, print "Graph Check: " + hasCycle(n).
mistakes: Forgetting the parent parameter - every two-node connection looks like a cycle.
Checking the whole graph from vertex 0 only - missed components hide cycles.
Returning "No Cycle" too early inside the component loop.
note: Star graph (4 edges from 0) has no cycle; 0-1-2-3-4-1 has one.

title: BFS minimum hops from a source station
statement:
Banu is a metro planner who wants to know how many hops a passenger needs to reach every station from a starting station. The metro network has n stations numbered from 0 to n-1, and every track joins two stations and can be used in both directions. One hop means travelling along one track. The function bfs finds the minimum number of hops from the starting station to every station, and stores -1 for a station that cannot be reached. The network is stored in an adjacency matrix.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v. Last line: integer source.
Output Format: n lines: "Distance of <i>: " + minimum hops (or -1 if unreachable).
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2).
easy: Standard BFS: start the queue with the source at distance 0; every newly discovered neighbour gets distance + 1; unreachable stations keep -1.
logic: Set dist[i] = -1 for everyone, then dist[source] = 0 and enqueue the source.
Pop u; for every neighbour v with dist[v] == -1: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 and enqueue.
The dist[v] == -1 test doubles as the visited check.
algorithm: bfs(int n, int source): queue array, front = rear = 0; initialise dist; enqueue source.
while (front < rear): u = dequeue; scan v = 0..n-1; if adj and dist[v] == -1 -> update and enqueue.
main: read graph and source; call bfs; print "Distance of <i>: " << dist[i] for each station.
mistakes: Marking visited only when POPPING from the queue (a vertex can be enqueued twice and get wrong distances).
Setting dist[source] = 1 or forgetting dist[source] = 0.
Initialising dist to 0 instead of -1 (then unreachable stations print 0).
note: Source note: the sample-output column is blank in the QB; outputs below were computed with the verified program and marked INFERRED.

title: Prim's minimum spanning tree from vertex 0
statement:
Elango is an engineer who plans to connect n villages numbered from 0 to n-1 with internet cables. A cable can be laid between some pairs of villages, and every possible cable has a cost. He wants every village to be connected to every other village, directly or through other villages, with the smallest possible total cost of the cables. The given possible cables always connect all the villages. The program stores the possible cables in an adjacency matrix, where 0 means that the cable between two villages is not possible, and the function primMST uses Prim's method, starting from the village 0, to find the smallest total cost.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v, w (possible cable with cost w).
Output Format: "MST Weight: " + smallest total cost.
Constraints: 2 <= n <= 15; n-1 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2); 1 <= w <= 100; graph connected; no self-loops or duplicate cables.
easy: Grow the tree from village 0: repeatedly pick the cheapest edge from any tree vertex to any outside vertex, add that cost, and update the best known key for outside vertices.
logic: key[v] = cheapest edge cost connecting v to the current tree (infinity at first, key[0] = 0).
Each round picks the unvisited vertex u with the smallest key, adds key[u] to total, and relaxes its edges.
After n rounds every vertex is in the tree and total is the MST weight.
algorithm: Initialise key[] = huge, inTree[] = false, key[0] = 0, total = 0.
Repeat n times: find the smallest-key unvisited u; inTree[u] = true; total += key[u];
for every v: if graph[u][v] > 0 and not inTree[v] and graph[u][v] < key[v] -> key[v] = graph[u][v].
Print "MST Weight: " + total.
mistakes: Picking the smallest edge GLOBALLY instead of edges leaving the tree (Prim grows from the tree).
Adding graph[u][v] instead of key[v] to the total.
Missing the inTree check when relaxing - tree vertices would get re-added.
note: Second sample's MST uses edges 0-4(6), 4-1(5), 4-3(8)... precisely 6+5+8+3 = 22.

title: Dijkstra shortest distances with INF output
statement:
Dilip runs a courier service in a region with n towns numbered from 0 to n-1. Every road joins two towns, can be used in both directions, and has a length in kilometers. The program stores the roads in an adjacency matrix, where 0 means that there is no road. The function dijkstra finds the length of the shortest route from the starting town to every town, using Dijkstra's method, and the function printDistances prints the lengths, with "INF" for a town that cannot be reached from the starting town.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v, w. Last line: source.
Output Format: "Distances:" followed by " value" for every town (or " INF").
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2); 1 <= w <= 100; no self-loops or duplicate roads.
easy: Dijkstra: repeatedly confirm the closest unfinished town, then relax its outgoing roads; unreachable towns print INF.
logic: dist[] starts at a huge value; dist[source] = 0.
Each round picks the unfinished town with the smallest finite distance, marks it done, and relaxes its neighbours.
dist[u] + graph[u][v] < dist[v] triggers the update.
Print " INF" for towns still at the huge value.
algorithm: dijkstra(n, source, dist): initialise; loop n times: pick u; if u == -1 break; done[u] = true; relax neighbours.
printDistances: "Distances:" then " dist[i]" or " INF" per town.
main: read graph and source; run; print.
mistakes: Selecting towns whose distance is still INFINITY as the minimum (guard with dist[v] != huge or break).
Relaxing with a road weight of 0 (0 means NO road in the matrix).
Printing INF as 1000000000 - the output must literally show INF.
note: Sample 1: distances 0 2 5 6 (town 3 reached via 2 with cost 1).

title: Minimum semesters (layered topological sort)
statement:
Dr. Fathima is the academic coordinator of a college that offers n courses numbered from 0 to n-1. Some courses have a prerequisite: "a b" means that the course a must be completed in an earlier semester before the course b can be taken. In every semester, a student takes all the courses whose prerequisites are already completed in the earlier semesters, and no other course. A course taken in a semester does not help the courses of the same semester. Write a program that prints the minimum number of semesters needed to complete all the courses. If the prerequisites contain a cycle, so that some course can never be taken, print a message.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: a, b (a is a prerequisite of b).
Output Format: "Semesters: " + count, or "Impossible: Cycle in prerequisites".
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)); no self-loops or repeated prerequisites.
easy: Layer-by-layer removal: every semester all courses with zero remaining prerequisites are taken together; if a round finds no such course, there is a cycle.
logic: Build the directed adjacency matrix and in-degrees.
Each round: collect ALL courses with indeg == 0 and not done (this is the semester batch).
Empty batch with courses left -> cycle -> print the Impossible message.
Mark the batch done, decrement each successor's indegree, semesters++.
algorithm: Read edges; set adj[a][b] = 1 and indeg[b]++ (guarding duplicates).
while taken < n: gather batch; if batch empty -> print Impossible and return.
For each u in batch: done[u] = true; taken++; for each j with adj[u][j] == 1: indeg[j]--.
semesters++; after the loop print "Semesters: " + semesters.
mistakes: Taking one course per semester instead of the whole zero-indegree batch (the sample expects 2, not 4).
Decrementing indegrees BEFORE printing... rather: updating batch members' indegrees within the same round must not enable same-semester chains (the batch is fixed first, then all decrements happen).
Missing the duplicate-edge guard (two identical prerequisites would double-decrement).
note: Sample: 5 courses, edges 0->1 and 2->3 -> semester 1: {0,2,4}, semester 2: {1,3} -> Semesters: 2.

title: Two debate teams (bipartite check with BFS colouring)
statement:
Ilango is a teacher who has to split n students numbered from 0 to n-1 into two debate teams, Team A and Team B. Some pairs of students are close friends, and he does not want two close friends to be in the same team, because they tend to agree on everything. Every student must be in exactly one team. Write a program that finds out whether such a split is possible. To make the answer unique, process the students from the smallest number to the largest. Every student who is not yet placed and is processed gets Team A, and the friends of a student placed in one team must be placed in the other team. Print the teams if the split is possible.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v (close friends).
Output Format: "Possible", then "Team A:" + numbers, then "Team B:" + numbers; or just "Not Possible".
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2); no self-loops or repeated pairs.
easy: This is graph 2-colouring: BFS from every unplaced student (Team A = colour 0), give every friend the opposite colour, and fail when two friends already share a colour.
logic: color[i] = -1 means unplaced.
For each start in increasing order: if unplaced, colour it 0 and BFS.
Neighbour uncoloured -> colour 1 - color[u] and enqueue; neighbour with the SAME colour -> print Not Possible and stop.
Otherwise print Possible and list Team A (colour 0) and Team B (colour 1) in increasing order.
algorithm: Read edges into adj matrix; colour array init -1.
For start = 0..n-1: if color[start] != -1 continue; colour[start] = 0; BFS queue.
BFS loop: u = dequeue; for v = 0..n-1 with adj[u][v]: if color[v] == -1 -> colour and enqueue; else if color[v] == color[u] -> print Not Possible; return.
Print "Possible", then Team A / Team B loops.
mistakes: Processing components out of order - the answer must be unique, so always take the smallest unplaced student first.
Printing teams after detecting a conflict - return immediately.
Forgetting that the queue must hold vertices across the whole component, not just the start.
note: Source note: the sample-output column is blank in the QB; outputs were computed with the verified program and marked INFERRED.

title: Bellman-Ford cheapest route with negative-cycle detection
statement:
Gokul plans a long drive from the city 0 to the city n-1 through n cities numbered from 0 to n-1. Some one-way roads have a toll, which is a positive cost, and some roads give a rebate, which is a negative cost. If a driver can reach a group of roads that forms a loop with a negative total cost, the driver could earn unlimited rebates by driving around it, so the cheapest cost is not defined. Write a program that prints the minimum total cost of travelling from the city 0 to the city n-1. If the city n-1 cannot be reached from the city 0, print "No Route". If a loop with a negative total cost can be reached from the city 0, print "Negative Cycle" instead.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v, w (one-way road with cost w, w != 0).
Output Format: "Negative Cycle", "No Route", or "Minimum Cost: " + cost.
Constraints: 2 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)); -50 <= w <= 100, w != 0; no self-loops or repeated roads.
easy: Bellman-Ford from city 0: relax every edge n-1 times; one extra relaxation pass detects negative cycles; then report the cost to city n-1.
logic: dist[0] = 0, everyone else infinity.
Repeat (n - 1) passes over ALL edges relaxing dist[v] = dist[u] + w when better.
One more pass: any further improvement reachable from 0 -> Negative Cycle.
dist[n-1] still infinity -> No Route; else print Minimum Cost.
algorithm: Store edges in arrays eu[], ev[], ew[].
for pass = 1..n-1: for each edge: relax if dist[u] finite and better.
for each edge: if still relaxable (from a finite dist) -> print Negative Cycle; return.
If dist[n-1] == INF print "No Route"; else print "Minimum Cost: " << dist[n-1].
mistakes: Running only one relaxation pass - negative edges need the full n-1 rounds to settle.
Detecting the cycle without checking reachability from city 0 (an unreachable negative loop must NOT trigger the message).
Reporting Minimum Cost when n-1 is unreachable.
note: Sample 1: 0->2 costs 3, then 2->1 costs -5 (dist[1] = -2), but the target city 2 stays at 3 -> Minimum Cost: 3.

title: Connected components: count, largest size, connectivity
statement:
Hemalatha works for a telecom company that has built phone lines between the villages of a district. There are n villages numbered from 0 to n-1, and every phone line joins two villages and works in both directions. Two villages are in the same group if they can talk to each other, directly or through other villages. A village with no phone line forms a group alone. The network is called connected if all the villages are in one group. Write a program that prints the number of groups of villages, the number of villages in the largest group, and whether the network is connected.
Input Format: Line 1: integers n and m. Next m lines: u, v (a phone line).
Output Format: "Components: " + count; "Largest Component: " + size; "Connected: Yes/No".
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 15; 0 <= m <= min(50, n(n-1)/2); no self-loops or repeated lines.
easy: DFS from every unvisited village; each new DFS start is one component; remember the size of the biggest component.
logic: dfs(u) marks u visited and returns 1 + sum of DFS sizes of unvisited neighbours.
Main loop: every unvisited vertex starts a new component; count++ and track largest.
components == 1 -> Connected: Yes.
algorithm: Read graph into adj matrix.
For i = 0..n-1: if not visited: size = dfs(i); components++; largest = max(largest, size).
Print Components / Largest Component / Connected lines.
mistakes: Counting a component per EDGE instead of per unvisited start vertex.
Forgetting isolated villages (m = 0) - each is its own component of size 1.
Comparing component size with largest using >= (ties must keep the FIRST largest - irrelevant for the value, but > is cleaner).
note: Samples recovered from the image embedded in the QB (see audit).
